links.outcome: Patient satisfaction, usefulness, feeling cared for by AI vs human vs no disclosure of message authorship
links.effect: AI disclosure lowered satisfaction slightly vs human disclosure (0.13; 95% CI 0.05-0.22) and vs no disclosure (0.09; 95% CI 0.01-0.17); >75% satisfied regardless of disclosure.
links.quote: The mean change in score between AI and human disclosure was 0.13 (95% CI, 0.05-0.22) points for satisfaction, favoring human disclosure, and 0.09 (95% CI, 0.01-0.17) points for satisfaction between AI and no disclosure, favoring no disclosure.

links.outcome: Preference among AI disclosure statements for portal messages; satisfaction with disclosure
links.effect: Most preferred statement (33%) was the shortest: 'written by Dr. T. with the support of automated tools'; disclosure caused only small satisfaction reduction, with >75% satisfied.
links.quote: The AI disclosure statement that received the highest proportion of most preferred (33%) was, “This message was written by Dr. T. with the support of automated tools” (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 ).

links.outcome: Patient reactions to and preferences among AI disclosure wording variants
links.effect: Evaluated reactions to disclosure; 893 (61.4%) ranked five disclosure versions; brief statement preferred; disclosure did not greatly reduce satisfaction.
links.quote: Participants preferred the shortest disclosure statement, which stated, “This message was written by Dr T. with the support of automated tools,” a takeaway that we are implementing at our health system.

links.effect: Satisfied/strongly satisfied: 857/1099 (78.0%) computer disclosure, 897/1108 (81.0%) no disclosure, and 895/1092 (82.0%) human disclosure.
links.quote: Most respondents agreed or strongly agreed with the statement “I am satisfied with the interaction,” regardless of disclosure (897 of 1108 [81.0%] for no disclosure, 857 of 1099 [78.0%] for computer disclosure, and 895 of 1092 [82.0%] for human disclosure) ( Figure 4 ).
